title: BFS And DFS Interview Patterns Questionnaire
concept: Graph traversal interview selection and tradeoffs

questions.prompt: Match each grid graph term to its Number Of Islands meaning.
questions.explanation: Translating the grid into nodes, edges, and components makes the required traversal direct.

questions.prompt: Why are BFS and DFS both correct for counting islands?

options.label: Both can visit every cell in one connected component before the outer scan continues.
Both always find identical shortest paths through an island.
Both sort land cells before visiting them.

questions.explanation: The answer depends on complete component discovery, not the internal order used to visit that component.

questions.prompt: Fill the traversal that guarantees the first discovered equal-cost shortest route.
questions.template: For the minimum number of moves in an unweighted graph, start with {{blank}}.
questions.explanation: BFS processes every route of distance d before it processes any route of distance d plus one.

questions.prompt: Order the DFS color states for a course with no detected cycle.
questions.explanation: An edge to a visiting node is a back edge; a complete node has already been proven cycle-free.

questions.prompt: What tells Kahn's BFS topological algorithm that the prerequisite graph contains a cycle?

options.label: It processes fewer courses than the total number of courses.
Its initial queue contains every course.
A course receives a negative indegree.

questions.explanation: Nodes in or behind a cycle never reach zero indegree, so they cannot all be removed from the graph.

questions.prompt: On a huge solid grid, what practical risk most clearly distinguishes recursive DFS from iterative BFS?

options.label: Recursive DFS can overflow the runtime call stack.
Recursive DFS necessarily counts the island incorrectly.
BFS changes every grid edge into a weighted edge.

questions.explanation: Both algorithms are correct, but an enormous recursive path can exceed language call-stack limits.
